# **M2 — Dark.Tyro: a four-line change that cuts photo damage by 74%**

**Team Dark.Tyro** · Echo Zhao · Nissa Corlidea

**Theme 2 (Text-to-Image) · Dark / attack side** · Milestone 2

**In short.** IMPRESS washes the whole photo to strip a protective shield. Most of that work is wasted, because an image editor repaints half the picture anyway. We wash only the part the editor keeps. Photo damage drops **74%**, and recovery is no worse than a wash that runs **ten times longer**. This is a two-image pilot (`n = 2`), so read it as early evidence, not a settled result. Our **Tyro Wash Test** is open: edit one function to enter.

---

## **1 · Code and how to run it**

* Main notebook: [**Dark\_Tyro\_M2.ipynb**](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1pir9s-u8zhW0PSIGWaGiM5wHykt2GJX3?usp=drive_link)
* Starter code for defenders: [**Tyro\_Wash\_Test\_STARTER.ipynb**](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1RzeHQgHGMSKqDUGbCV3jdMY2d5-rBdVU?usp=drive_link)
* Metric checks, optional: [**Tyro\_M2\_diagnostics.ipynb**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hwwN1js5_VbhCogRU0Ue-XMsW8ub3_Wg/view?usp=drive_link)

**Environment.** Google Colab, one T4 GPU. Run the notebook top to bottom; dependencies are pinned in the setup cell. Every result below comes from a single cold run with the outputs saved in the notebook, so you can read the numbers without running anything.

**To reproduce §5:** `seed = 0`, shield fixed at `pg_iters = 40, pg_grad_reps = 2, pg_eps = 16`, and the two 512 × 512 faces and masks from the challenge pack. A smoke switch in the config cell runs the whole path in about four minutes at reduced settings — use it to check your setup first. It prints a warning, and its numbers mean nothing.

The change itself is one line:

`purified_v2 = mask * purified_impress + (1 - mask) * protected`

**What `mask = 1` means here:** the pixels the editor **keeps**. It is the opposite of the repaint mask you hand the editor. We measured this rather than assumed it (§3) — reversed, the method does the opposite of what we claim. The mask is blurred at the edge, because a hard line between washed and unwashed pixels is itself a visible artefact.

---

## **2 · How the pipeline works**

clean photo

    ↓  PROTECT — PhotoGuard adds a small pattern

protected photo

    ↓  PURIFY — IMPRESS washes away the pattern

purified photo

    ↓  EDIT — Stable Diffusion inpainting uses a mask and prompt

edited photo

    ↓  MEASURE — score edit recovery and photo quality

two results

**The defence.** [PhotoGuard](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.06588) (Salman et al., ICML 2023) adds a faint pattern to a photo. A person sees no change, but the editor's encoder reads the image wrongly, so the edit comes out garbled. We use the paper's cheaper **encoder attack**, which targets the autoencoder only.

**The attack we build on.** [IMPRESS](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19248) (Cao et al., NeurIPS 2023, [code](https://github.com/AAAAAAsuka/Impress)) starts from a weakness in that shield: **a protected photo no longer survives a round trip through the autoencoder.** We checked this ourselves and measured a round-trip error of **0.0204** for protected photos against **0.0071** for clean ones. The shield is invisible to us but not to the model.

So IMPRESS looks for the nearest image the autoencoder does accept:

`min ‖D(E(x′)) − x′‖² + λ‖x′ − x_prot‖²`

The first term pushes the image back into shape, which is what removes the shield. The second stops it drifting into a different picture altogether.

**Where the waste is.** That search covers **every pixel**, because IMPRESS was written to protect a whole image. Inpainting does not work on the whole image — it keeps one region and repaints the rest. Cleaning pixels the editor is about to throw away buys nothing and costs picture quality. That is the gap we go after.

---

## **3 · What we changed**

First we measured how much of the photo the editor actually keeps. Comparing a clean photo with its edit, we took the mean absolute difference per pixel on 8-bit greyscale, inside and outside the kept region. Across the two test images: the **kept region moved 4–7 levels**, the **repainted region moved 86–96**. That measurement is also what tells us which way round the mask goes.

So we wash only the kept region and leave the protected pixels everywhere else, blending across a soft edge. The prediction:

> Recovery should hold up, because the wash still covers everything the editor keeps. Photo damage should drop, because the wash no longer touches pixels that get repainted.

**The risk we had to test.** The repainted region is thrown away as *output*, but the editor still reads the whole image as *context*. A shield left outside the mask could therefore still steer what gets generated. If recovery had fallen, this is why it would have fallen.

The change costs nothing: version C runs the same 100 wash steps as version A.

---

## **4 · What we measure**

| Metric | Plain meaning | Better |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **`R_pipe`** | How much of the shield's damage to the edit the wash undid | Higher |
| **`LPIPS`** | How different the photo looks from the original | Lower |

`R_pipe = (SSIM_pur − SSIM_adv) / (1 − SSIM_adv)`. Both SSIM values compare an **edited** image against the **edited clean** image — not against the original photo. So `R_pipe` asks: *did the editor end up producing what it would have produced with no shield in the way?* 1.0 means yes entirely, 0 means the shield held. We write it as a percentage, so 14.48% means 0.1448. Values are not capped.

⚠️ **Two different things in this project are called SSIM.** `R_pipe` uses SSIM between *edited* images. The LPIPS column answers a separate question — whether the photograph itself survived.

**Where this metric is weak.** The bottom of the fraction, `1 − SSIM_adv`, is the shield's measured effect on the edit. A shield that barely disturbs the edit makes that number tiny, and then `R_pipe` is small differences divided by almost nothing. It can even go negative. §6 shows this is a live problem at our settings, which is why our challenge scorer checks that a shield registers before it reports a score.

**`R_pipe` does not say whether the edit was any good.** It only says whether the pipeline behaved as it would have without a shield. Whether the output matches the prompt is a separate CLIPScore measure (`R_edit`) in the diagnostics notebook, and the two are allowed to disagree.

We always report both numbers. A wash that gains recovery while losing picture quality is a trade, not an improvement.

---

## **5 · Results**

Four versions, one shield setting, the same two faces, the same seed. **`n = 2` images.**

| Version | Wash | `R_pipe` % ↑ | LPIPS vs clean ↓ |
| :---- | :---- | ----: | ----: |
| N | none — the starting point | 0.00 | 0.017 |
| A | IMPRESS, 100 steps — the M1 baseline | 9.51 | 0.150 |
| B | IMPRESS, 1000 steps — the paper's budget | 13.54 | 0.108 |
| **C** | **ours:** IMPRESS, 100 steps, kept region only | **14.48** | **0.038** |

![][image1]

**The picture quality result.** C cuts LPIPS from A's 0.150 to 0.038 at the same compute — a **74% drop**. Measured as damage above the no-wash floor of 0.017 it is 84%. We quote the 74% figure throughout. Against B, C causes 64% less damage.

**The recovery result.** C and B are **0.94 points apart**, which is inside our measured noise floor, so we treat them as the same. That is the finding: **C reaches the paper's full 1000-step result using 100 steps and doing a third of the damage.** C is 4.97 points above A, which is just past the 4-point line we set ourselves — suggestive, but with `n = 2` we do not call it established.

**What the pictures show.**

![][image2]

Left to right: the edit of the clean photo, then the edit of the protected photo — the shield has smeared the chin and jaw. `N_no_wash` is identical to it, which is the null version behaving correctly. A and B both clear the smearing but land on a different scene (green field, changed headphones). C stays closest to the clean edit, keeping the window and the headphones, with a faint line left on the chin. **C is not artefact-free**, and the scene differences in A and B are a reminder that some of what `R_pipe` measures is ordinary generator variation, not shield removal (§6).

**Per-image spread.** Measured separately on each face, recovery is `A [8.8, 7.4]`, `B [11.4, 13.9]`, `C [16.1, 8.5]`. All positive, but **C's two images are 7.6 points apart against A's 1.4** — C's advantage is real and also much less consistent. With two images we cannot say which face is typical. These per-image values use scikit-image's SSIM, which reads about 0.01 higher than the pipeline's own SSIM, so use them for spread rather than as absolute figures.

**On replication.** Re-running one configuration on the same hardware reproduces LPIPS exactly while `R_pipe` moves 2–4 points. The cause is worth stating: half-precision kernel selection shifts the protected photo by **0.1 of a grey level**, and the editor turns that into about **11 levels** of output — roughly 100×. *Our metric is unstable for the same reason the defence works.* Moving between platforms moved it further: the same versions run earlier on Kaggle scored 4–7 points lower across the board, because the shield happened to bite less hard there. Comparisons inside one run are sound; figures across runs are not.

---

## **6 · A check that limits what we can claim**

We tested `R_pipe` against the generator's ordinary randomness. We edited each clean photo twice, changing only the seed, with no protection anywhere. Lower SSIM means a bigger change.

| Image | Different seed | PhotoGuard shield |
| :---- | ----: | ----: |
| 1233476865\_1 | 0.472 | 0.584 |
| 1525918600\_1 | 0.415 | 0.610 |

Changing the seed alters the edit **more** than the shield does. So the generator's own randomness may be as large as the effect `R_pipe` is supposed to isolate. That limits how far any single `R_pipe` figure can be pushed. It does not prove the results table is contaminated, since all four versions there share one seed.

Doubling the shield-strength setting changed nothing. That hints the setting may be inactive on this code path, but it does not prove it — a saturated or weakly connected setting would look the same.

This is why we treat the picture-quality result as solid and the recovery result as provisional. Full test in `Tyro_M2_diagnostics.ipynb`.

## **7 · Tyro Wash Test**

**Build a shield our wash cannot remove.** Entry needs one function: `protect()`.

**What you get.** 📦 [**tyro\_wash\_test\_trackA.zip**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1fiZshDbJeL2PzkJGT551LJH3G7o4CDJR/view?usp=drive_link) (3.6 MB) — 10 clean 512 × 512 faces, their masks, and `check_submission.py`. 📓 [**Tyro\_Wash\_Test\_STARTER.ipynb**](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1RzeHQgHGMSKqDUGbCV3jdMY2d5-rBdVU?usp=drive_link).

**What you do.** Edit `protect()`. Tune the PhotoGuard protector we include, or replace it with your own. Send back 10 PNGs at 512 × 512 with our filenames. That is the whole interface — your method stays private, we score only the images.

**How we score it.** We run our purifier over your images, then edit the clean, protected and purified versions with the **same prompt, seed and mask**, and publish two numbers: **`R_pipe`** (how much of the edit our wash restores — you want it low) and **`LPIPS(protected, clean)`** (how much your shield changes the photo — you want it low too; AlexNet backbone, as in `check_submission.py`, since another backbone gives another number).

**Both numbers go on one chart.** Judging robustness alone has an obvious cheat: perturb until the photo is noise, and nothing can wash it off — but nothing can edit it either. That entry lands in the top-right corner and we will say so.

**To be ranked, keep mean LPIPS at or below 0.10** across the ten images. The figure comes from `pur_eps = 0.1`, the picture-quality allowance inside IMPRESS's own objective — which is a soft penalty weighted at `pur_alpha = 0.01`, not a hard limit, so treat it as a guide rather than a matched budget. Our own PhotoGuard reference scores 0.0665, so there is room. Entries above the limit are still plotted and discussed, just not ranked.

**We check your shield registers first.** A shield that barely disturbs the edit turns `R_pipe` into noise (§4), so we test for that before reporting a score. This replaces our M1 rule of SSIM ≤ 0.85, which we published before measuring anything. The measured seed floor across the ten images runs **0.285 to 0.707**, so 0.85 would have passed everything. `check_submission.py` does the format and LPIPS checks on your machine; `R_pipe` scoring runs on ours.

**Timing.** The ten images are the evaluation set, and the edit prompt and seed are fixed and published in the starter notebook. Reply here if the pack needs fixing and we will update it promptly. Every result goes into a follow-up, including entries that beat ours.

## **8 · Team we engaged with: Light.Cyber Ninjas (ESD-x)**

**What we targeted: the assumption behind their next step.**

[Light.Cyber Ninjas](https://edstem.org/au/courses/37864/discussion/3535833) erase Van Gogh's style from Stable Diffusion v1-4 using **ESD-x** (Gandikota et al., ICCV 2023), which retrains cross-attention so a phrase stops reaching its visual style. Their next step is to erase **several descriptions** instead of one — their fork now has an `--erase_concept_variants` flag. That step assumes something testable: that more descriptions cover more of the ways a user can ask for the style.

**1. The erasure is taught at points.** ESD learns from the model's own response to one phrase. Four descriptions teach four points. Whether the space between them is covered is a question for experiment, not something the method guarantees.

**2. Their test set does not test their own question.** They ask whether the style comes back through *multilingual* prompts. Their one multilingual test row is a French **description**, not the artist's name in another language. We are not claiming the translated name defeats the defence — only that nothing currently measures it.

**3. We tried a cheap way to predict which routes survive, and it failed.** We embedded candidate prompts with the CLIP text encoder that SD v1-4 uses, and measured distance to their five planned erase targets — four ways: ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/32, each summarised two standard ways. **The ordering is not stable.** Two summaries of the *same* encoder agree at Spearman **ρ = +0.03**:

| route | L/14 mean-token | L/14 pooled |
| :---- | ----: | ----: |
| 梵高 (Chinese name) | 0.326 | 0.441 |
| ゴッホ (Japanese name) | 0.345 | 0.499 |
| фан гог (Russian) | 0.217 | 0.430 |
| Paul Cezanne (never erased) | 0.545 | 0.487 |

One summary puts the non-English names furthest from "Van Gogh"; the other puts them mid-pack. So the narrow conclusion: **these embeddings do not give a stable ranking of candidate bypass prompts, and distance in prompt space is not enough on its own to choose which variants to erase.** Settling it takes generated images — our Milestone 3 work.

**4. One comparison was stable, and it is worth their attention.** Within each of the four setups, where both sides are measured the same way, their **control prompt** sits within **0.05** of the nearest candidate attack route against their five erase targets. Their control is not well separated from what they plan to erase. That does not prove erasure will damage it — it is a reason to check with generated images, since preserving unrelated styles is their second goal.

**5. A practical note.** Their §6 says training is deliberately not run yet, so there is no erased model published and no entry to their challenge can be scored. The ESD authors publish pre-erased, diffusers-ready UNets at `erasing.baulab.info/weights/esd_models/`, including `diffusers-VanGogh-ESDx1-UNET.pt` — their exact method, concept and base model, with no training needed.

**Why we looked here.** Our own result has the same shape. PhotoGuard spreads its protection over the whole photo, and we found most of that buys nothing because the editor repaints the region anyway. Both defences cover less ground than their framing suggests. We also ran into the same measurement problem twice — in §6 with our own metric, and in point 3 with a text-space shortcut.

We have posted this on their thread with the full table, and offered to run the image test against the pre-erased model and publish whatever it shows, including a result in their favour.

---

## **9 · What we are not claiming**

* `n = 2` images, one shield setting, one seed. The picture-quality gap is large and consistent. The recovery gap over A is only just past our own noise line, and C's two images are 7.6 points apart, so no single recovery figure should be read as typical.
* `R_pipe` becomes unreliable when a shield barely registers, and §6 shows the generator's randomness is comparable to the shield's effect here. Read `R_pipe` as an ordering within one run, not as a number that travels.
* LPIPS over the whole image cannot show *where* the improvement happens. Our method is specifically about regions, so measuring LPIPS separately inside and outside the mask is the right next step, and we have not done it.
* Our mask is the same mask the editor uses. A defender who does not publish the mask makes this attack harder — a fair defence to try in the challenge.
* §8 contains no generated images. Points 1, 2 and 5 are about method and test design, point 3 is a negative result about a shortcut, and only point 4 is a measured claim — within one setup, not across setups.

**Next.** Raise `n`, measure LPIPS inside and outside the mask separately, sweep shield strength on a code path where the setting works, and publish the Wash Test leaderboard.
